(1) advanced L1 English–L2 French learners encode /y/– /u/ and mid rounded vowels /œ/– /ɔ/ in their phonological representations, but (2) they do not use these distinctions in their phonetic categorization, and (3) the lexical encoding of these contrasts in L2 phonology is not a necessary condition for accurate phonetic categorization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the acquisition and representation of the French front vs. back vowel contrast by English learners.
how learners map acoustics to the phonological system of a second language, with a particular emphasis on the acquisition of front rounded vowels.
the relationship between lexical representations, the lexicon and the phonological system, and the acquisition of the phonology of L2.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in L2 acquisition of French vowels, the lexical encoding of the /y/ vs /u/ contrast is acquired earlier than that of the /œ/ vs /ɔ/ contrast, which is acquired later than phonetic categorization of both contrasts.

the advanced learners have phonetic categories that are distinct from native speaker categories and phonological representations that are distinct from the native speaker representations, but the learners’ representations are not distinct from the native speakers’ categories.
the learners’ phonetic categorization of French vowels is not yet adult-like, and that their lexical representation of French front vs. back vowels may be incomplete.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the acquisition of French front rounded vowels in English speakers is not as difficult as previously thought, as long as the learners are exposed to a large amount of French input and are able to acquire the French vowel contrasts in their phonetic categorization system.

the DMAP approach is a viable alternative to the traditional view that phonological representations are built on the basis of phonetic categories, which are in turn constructed from acoustic information.
the learners’ phonological representations are directly mapped onto the acoustics of the target language, but that this mapping does not necessarily lead to phonetic categorization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
phonetic categorization does not depend on the phonological representation of a given phoneme in the L2.
the phonetic and phonological representations of L2 speakers may not be as closely aligned as previously assumed, with the former being more accurate and the latter more variable.
, while the acquisition of phonetic categorization is an important goal in second language (L2) learning, the acquisition of lexical representations is also critical.
